rv.q: You can't take your eyes off him.

The revival of David Mamet's 1975 drama about three small-time crooks plotting a coin heist is a master class in profanity and paranoia, with Sam Rockwell, Laurence Fishburne and Darren Criss delivering performances that crackle with desperate energy.
This crackling revival of “American Buffalo” highlights by contrast the devolution of Mamet’s craft that coincided with the shift in his worldview, from red-diaper baby to apologist for billionaires.
The stuttering, overlapping rhythms no longer startle – the style was co-opted and spread far and wide ages ago by just about every post
Every line of dialogue, expertly delivered not only by McAvoy but a large and flawless ensemble, is either a delight, an arrow, or both
Because American Buffalo works as it used to work (or at least every time I’ve seen it) as a vivid comic indictment of warped American posturing and language.
Much of the play, especially the language, is dated and therefore cringe-inducing.
Audiences will have fun here, as they usually do with this play.
The three actors bring distinct energy and interpretive approaches to their roles.
But the ugliness in Mamet’s talk is not just stale and cheap, it’s onerous and inexcusable.
How else to explain the absence of menace or pity or recognizable human feeling in the finely acted Broadway revival of American Buffalo, directed by Neil Pepe at Circle in the Square?
The brilliant acting and the sublime direction of Neil Pepe will leave you gratified.
Rockwell and Fishburne are definitely worth the price of admission.
That shouldn't stop anyone from seeing this superbly acted production of one of his most important plays.

Directed with verve by Tony-nominated Neil Pepe, this American Buffalo is a solid enough reenactment of Mamet’s imperfect play, worthy of a visit even by liberals dismayed by the playwright’s politics.

The three-man cast, led by Laurence Fishburne, Sam Rockwell and Darren Criss, brings depth and humanity to Mamet's profanity-laden characters in this Circle in the Square Theatre revival.

However, the in-the-round stage at Circle in the Square is a consistent treat of a setting to see such actors letting loose so intimately, particularly Rockwell, whose freewheeling menace and blunt nonchalance should be deemed Tony nomination-worthy.

Delayed for two years due to the COVID-19 pandemic and set in an indeterminate urban landscape of the semi-recent past, this “American Buffalo” lacks the granularity and specificity to say much of anything, let alone make a case for its creator’s continued relevance.
Otherwise stay home and watch TV.
If there was a “blue book” for plays, as there are for coins, I suspect one would see quite a drop in value for “American Buffalo” since its premiere.

There’s nothing wrong with plays in which not much happens, but with Laurence Fishburne, Sam Rockwell, and Darren Criss up for sale, there’s no reason for this Neil Pepe-directed revival to lowball an audience this badly.
Perhaps the real tragedy is the fact that American Buffalo remains relevant today at all.

tn.cat: Best Scenic Design of a Play

cn.t: Critics are divided on this Mamet revival: some praise the stellar cast (Fishburne, Rockwell, Criss) for elevating the profane dialogue, while others find the 1975 play dated and question its relevance in 2022.

sg.ra: In the 3/4 thrust configuration these front rows put you at the lip of the playing area with actors entering from aisles directly beside you. Headout notes rows AA-B are 'closest to the stage' and audiences are 'roped into the play's action.' Because the stage is surrounded on three sides, the acting is deliberately blocked so no front row gets a sustained back-of-actor view, but individual moments will face away from you — that is inherent to in-the-round and not a flaw of this section.

Universally cited as the optimal vantage in this thrust venue — close enough to feel the intimacy of a 776-seat room with only 10 rows, but one row back from the front so sightlines catch the whole three-sided playing area. Headout: 'Center Orchestra - rows B, C and D' positioned centrally are 'possibly the best seats in the house.' The in-the-round blocking is designed so these central rows at eye-level with the floor see choreography and staging as intended.

Because the venue only has 10 rows total and stadium-inclined seating, rows H-I still feel close to the thrust while giving elevated sightlines that reveal staging patterns on the floor — useful for musicals with choreography. Headout: 'Rows H and I in the upper middle level offer a great view of the stage and the prices are lower than those of the premium orchestra seats.' AVFMS reviewer MusicaltheatreWhiz in H144 (Just in Time, Feb 2026): 'There really isn't a bad seat in the house!' TripAdvisor: 'up is better for musicals.'

In a typical Broadway house the last row would be a skip, but Circle in the Square is only 10 rows deep so row K is roughly where Row G would be in a standard theater. AVFMS danielb9 at K109 (Just in Time, Feb 28 2026): 'Enough legroom to be comfortable and despite being in the back row felt very connected to the action.' Multiple reviews note 'no obstruction' and 'great seat' for row K. Stadium incline ensures sightlines over heads. The in-the-round nature means some scenes still play toward the opposite side, but this is a venue property not a section flaw.

sg.n: Side Sections - Long Arms of the Horseshoe (100s & 200s)
sg.ra: The two long 'wide sides' of the horseshoe (the 100 and 200 numbered sections per BWW forum user Patash's question about 102/202 numbering) give a profile view of the main action. TripAdvisor: 'the two wide sides are fine' and are preferred over 'straight in front' which is 'too far from the rear end of the main stage.' AVFMS samr32 at C207 (Just in Time, Feb 26 2026): 'Amazing seat! Can see both stages so well, and the actors (including Jonathan Groff) run up and down the aisle right near you.' The 300-degree blocking means side sections regularly get face-forward moments; not behind-stage.

The one sustained warning across every source is the extreme corner seats where the horseshoe's ends meet the stage. Headout/TickPick specifically: 'seats 438-440 are obstructed when actors perform on the far left of the stage and vice versa for the opposite side' (437-439). Unlike the rest of the house where in-the-round angles are temporary, these corner positions can have whole extended scenes played entirely out of view on the opposite corner. In a 3/4 thrust with actors using the full perimeter, this is a structural flaw of the seat, not a temporary blocking issue.
